morning.title: FPI buying hits 5-year high in November. What's driving the $7.5 billion inflow?
morning.text: Mumbai: In a sharp U-turn after months of sustained selling, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) pumped $7.5 billion into Indian equities in the first 10 trading sessions of November - the highest monthly inflow in five years, according to Bloomberg data.This comes after FPIs withdrew $2.17 billion from Indian equities in October and $3.46 billion in September. The net investments in November so far are the highest since November 2021. The last time foreign investors pumped in more money in a single month was November 2020, when inflows stood at $9.56 billion, the data showed.135868866According to fund managers, FPIs have been aggressively investing amid a correction in AI-related stocks globally and a decline in crude oil prices. "The FPI flows are driven by multiple factors. profit booking on AI Investments, drop in oil prices, election results in Brazil, correction in Indian valuations over last two years, talks of exemptions on capital gains and reduction in rupee volatility," said Nilesh Shah, managing director of Kotak Mahindra AMC.All this came in quick succession and the combined effect is visible in FPI flows, he said.Read more: IPO calendar: Mahanadi Coalfields among 3 companies to raise over Rs 10,000 cr in busy week for primary marketBrent crude prices have fallen nearly 21% to $93.37 per barrel on November 13 from a peak of $118 on October 30. The Indian rupee has appreciated by ₹1.97, or about 2%, against the US dollar since the beginning of October, rising from ₹96.22 per dollar to ₹94.25 per dollar by mid-November.Domestic institutional investors, meanwhile, have turned net sellers, booking profits amid a sharp rally in the market, after providing a crucial backstop through much of the year. DIIs have sold equities worth over ₹49,000 crore in the first 10 trading sessions of November, according to NSE data. Since the beginning of November, the Sensex and Nifty have gained nearly 10% each, while the BSE MidCap 150 and BSE SmallCap 250 indices have advanced around 8% each.Read more: Will Sensex, Nifty continue their bull run or consolidate? 4 factors to watch out for this weekOverseas investors began 2026 with net outflows of $3.26 billion into Indian equities in January, before turning net buyers in February with investments of $1.69 billion. However, the respite was short-lived, as March saw a sharp reversal, with FPIs pulling out $13.23 billion - their biggest monthly sell-off.Their return to Indian equities reflects both global portfolio rotation away from AI-heavy markets and improving outlook for India, said Anurag Byas, director for global markets solutions at Rothschild & Co. "Lower crude prices, better earnings and now attractive valuations seem to have supported this sentiment change. This is a positive signal but may be early to be extrapolated; the fundamentals must improve and the oil and currency stability must hold for this to become a sustained trend," he said. Shah of Kotak Mahindra AMC expects FPI flows to move in line with how the above factors interplay with each other.

morning.title: Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China
morning.text:
Microsoft has announced massive price rises for commercial cloud services in India and New Zealand, but a substantial reduction in China.

The software giant sells its cloudy services in many local currencies, at an equivalent rate to the prices it charges in the USA.

As exchange rates shift, so do the prices Microsoft charges around the world.

Microsoft last week announced the new charges that will come into effect from January 1, 2027, and the news isn’t pleasant for customers in India, who face an increase of 15.7 percent for cloud services and up to 20 percent for some on-prem offerings. New Zealand customers face a ten percent price hike.

Customers in China, where Microsoft relies on a local partner called 21Vianet to deliver its cloud, will see costs fall by up to 8.5 percent.

Australian buyers will see costs fall by 4.5 percent. The only nation not in Asia on Microsoft’s list is Norway, where prices will ease 5.9 percent.

Sega Japan hits double trouble

Sega has just had a rotten week that saw it battle a data leak and an outage.

The outage impacted the company’s ALL.Net and Aime services, which connect arcade games across different locations. The services include administrative features for arcade operators, plus services for gamers including pre-payment to play, high score and profile recording, and networked gaming.

Sega suspended some ALL.Net and Aime services on November 1 after discovering unauthorized access to servers. At least thirteen games and services were then unavailable until around November 15.

The company hasn’t explained what went wrong, but assured customers the incident was not a data breach and that payment information was safe.

But data did leak for those who subscribe to some Sega newsletters. Sega uses a third-party outfit called Arara Co. to send some emails, and it leaked email addresses. No other personal data leaked from Arara. Sega has nonetheless warned newsletter recipients to watch out for suspicious messages.

Alibaba floats chip unit

Chinese tech giant Alibaba last week announced its intention to float its T-Head chip design biz on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

The filing announcing the spinoff describes T-Head as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China,” suggesting Alibaba doesn’t think buyers in the rest of the world are keen to acquire its chips.

T-Head going public “allows a more efficient deployment of Alibaba Group’s financial resources,” the filing states, and should also mean the chip design outfit can more easily find third-party customers.

India bans export of dead batteries

The government of India last week banned the export of “Lithium-Ion battery Black Mass” – a powdery substance created during the process of recycling batteries.

“It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese,” according to the government’s announcement of the ban, which argues the measure “will increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, thereby reducing import dependence and the associated foreign exchange outgo. It will also strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies.”

“Further, the measure will advance the circular economy and ‘urban mining’, reducing reliance on primary mining, while supporting environmentally sound recycling of this hazardous material within the country in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.”

Japanese giants to investigate orbiting datacenters

Five giant Japanese companies – NTT, Mitsubishi Electric, MUFG Bank, the Development Bank of Japan, and telco NTT DOCOMO – last week signed a memorandum of understanding that will see them jointly explore development and operation of a mega-constellation of satellites.

The five “will examine the technical and business feasibility of commercializing a diverse range of services enabled by mega-constellations, including communications, Earth observation, satellite-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), and space data centers.”

Mitsubishi already works with the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to jointly develop and manufacture rockets. The two banks regularly back big infrastructure projects, while the two NTT entities have advanced comms expertise.

The five companies didn’t set a deadline for delivery of a plan.

If they do decide there’s a business opportunity, they’ll likely need to look beyond Japan for launch capacity as JAXA does not currently possess a re-usable launch vehicle and operates at a modest launch cadence compared to private launch operators. ®

morning.title: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
morning.text:
United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.

The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military's national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday's mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX's Starlink. Sunday's failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.

Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.

Dems should call Trump’s immigration bluff
morning.text: In casting their ballots for Democrats, voters couldn’t have been clearer about their disgust with Republican Party priorities — including, as even President Donald Trump has admitted, his administration’s overzealous approach to immigration enforcement. “It might be too tough,” he told 60 Minutes last Sunday. Yet Trump has been anything but clear when asked what he plans to do about it.This past week alone, the president has veered from offering to work with Democrats on immigration reform to defending the promotion of immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff. Trump said targeting immigrants without criminal records “hurt” Republicans, but also said he’s not making changes. “There won’t be amnesty,” he told reporters. And that’s on top of his administration bragging about hitting new records for deportations. “Thanks to President Trump’s leadership,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “ICE has been unleashed.”ALSO READ | More companies may face action in H-1B probe, warns US Labour Department's Anthony D’EspositoGiven all the mixed messages, it seems highly unlikely that a fix for the nation’s broken immigration system is coming if Trump gets to dictate the agenda and the timetable. To be sure, a compromise would be ideal. But if anything is to get done on immigration in the next Congress, Democrats will likely have to force the issue, pushing legislation and daring Republicans to filibuster it or Trump to veto it.Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has proposed just such a strategy for making health care more affordable. Trump will have two choices, as Schumer told the Washington Sun. He will either sign what will be very popular legislation — “and he’ll know it’s popular” — or obstruct it, giving Democrats a better chance of winning the presidency in 2028.ALSO READ | IBM's H-1B move, US tech layoffs: Why is it getting harder for Indians to work and settle in America?The same could work for legislation on immigration reform (although it doesn’t seem to be a priority for the House so far). The key for Democrats will be resisting the temptation to go too far left, as some in the party want to do, and instead stick to policies that match public opinion and stand a good chance of improving the economy.Polls show that most Americans appreciate the economic benefits of legal immigration. They want a secure border, but don’t approve of violent enforcement tactics that have left multiple people dead. Americans also favor admitting refugees and asylum seekers fleeing war-torn countries, and providing a viable pathway to citizenship for immigrants who were brought to the US as children, or have been living in the US for years.Depending on the day, Trump will pay lip service to agreeing to much of this. As he told 60 Minutes last Sunday, killers should be deported, but not necessarily “good people working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel” and “paying taxes.”But Trump has said such things before, only to backtrack. He did so in 2017, when he toyed with helping DREAMers — immigrants brought to the US as children — get citizenship. What had seemed like a more solid deal fell apart in 2018 after immigration hard-liners, led by Miller, got involved. Another one fizzled in 2019.Trump has never been a particularly reliable negotiating partner. He breaks promises and changes his mind on a whim. With Miller in Trump’s ear more often now as White House chief of staff, Democrats are right to be skeptical that will change just because Republicans received an electoral beatdown for the ages. Yet Democrats seem to be moving forward anyway, however tentatively.This past week, a group of Latino lawmakers, many of them newly elected to Congress, gathered outside the Capitol to publicly push for immigration reform. Specifically, they called on Trump and Republicans to support the bipartisan Dignity Act and the American Dream and Promise Act, both of which would solve a mix of problems with the current immigration system.“I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform. But I am also a pragmatist,” Representative Veronica Escobar of Texas said. “And as we have — as we continue to have — Donald Trump in the White House, and without a supermajority in the Senate, we need Republican support. So any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan.”Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona said congressional Democrats had a responsibility to “protect as many families as possible,” even if that means “potentially cutting a deal with Donald Trump.”A smaller group of Latino business leaders who also spoke at the Capitol were more direct and, dare I say, more realistic. They reminded the Trump administration that its policy of mass deportations has disrupted the economy, forcing businesses to close and workers to stay home, forfeiting their paychecks. This has been as true in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas as it has been in southwestern Kansas. And it had a lot to do with Republican Latino voters abandoning Trump.In a warning to the administration, Benny Melendez, vice chair of the South Texas Builders Association, said to nods from Latino lawmakers: “If you want to continue harassing our communities, prepare yourself not only to lose your job, but get ready, because in the 2028 elections, these same communities you are now harassing will make sure you lose the White House.”The reality is, Trump may never compromise on legislation. That shouldn’t stop Democrats from advancing a vision of what a well-run immigration system could look like, and explaining how that could ease everything from the housing shortage that’s driving up costs to labor shortages at meatpacking plants and farms that threaten to raise grocery prices even more.If Democrats can present a plan that’s in line with what most Americans want, there’s a good chance voters will reward them for it — and punish Republicans for standing in the way. Just because the Trump administration is in disarray over immigration doesn’t mean Democrats have to be as well.The views expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the views of the publication.

morning.title: Inside Pakistan’s air-to-air missile arsenal: From Chinese PL-15s to indigenous Fa’az
morning.text:
New Delhi: Pakistan recently flight-tested its first indigenously developed air-to-air missile (AAM), named Fa’az (Urdu for victorious). The development marks a significant step for the country, which has so far relied primarily on Chinese- and US-made missiles. For India, the development merits attention, as recent standoffs between the two countries have been characterised by aerial engagements and Pakistan could potentially use the missile for a future conflict.
On 3 November, the day of the test, Pakistan military’s media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said, “The successful flight test underscores the technical maturity, innovation and self-reliance achieved by Pakistan’s defence industry.”
A video released by Pakistan showed the missile fitted onto a JF-17 Thunder, the fighter aircraft jointly developed by Pakistan and China.
Equipped with a state-of-the-art terminal guidance system, Fa’az is designed to engage enemy aerial targets at longer ranges, placing it in the category of Beyond-Visual-Range Air-to-Air Missiles (BVRAAMs). Importantly, the missile shown in the video was the passive imaging infrared (IIR) version, known as Fa’az IIR. A separate active radar-guided (RF) variant is also under development.
IIR missiles are tactically more effective as they use thermal imaging to build a two-dimensional image or silhouette of the target before locking on, rather than relying primarily on the heat signature of the target as older infrared (IR) missiles do.
The Fa’az IIR has an estimated detection range of 40 kilometres, while the RF version has a detection range of 25 km. Both variants are projected to have a range exceeding 100 km and a maximum speed of Mach 3.5 (supersonic).
The missile is being developed under Pakistan’s National Engineering and Scientific Commission (NESCOM) by the state-owned defence conglomerate Global Industrial and Defence Solutions (GIDS). The company first showcased mock-ups of both Fa’az variants at a defence exhibition in Istanbul, Turkey, in 2023. GIDS maintains that its products are developed locally and that it owns their intellectual property rights.
Pakistan has not released detailed information about Fa’az’s flight test or disclosed the development status of its radar-guided RF variant. Regardless of when the missile enters operational service, the test marks a significant step for Pakistan’s air defence industry.
Writing for The War Zone, a defence and military analysis website, Thomas Newdick described it as “a significant development in the country’s efforts to establish a domestic air-to-air weapons capability and join a relatively small group of countries with the expertise to develop such weapons”.
Also Read: Why Pakistan’s veteran power broker Maulana Fazlur Rehman is now challenging the military
Moving beyond American and Chinese missiles
Air Marshal Diptendu Choudhury (Retd), an airpower specialist and author affiliated with several Indian think-tanks, told ThePrint that Pakistan was dependent on the US for long, but started looking to China after America imposed sanctions on the sale of F-16s to Islamabad in 1990. “The Chinese helped Pakistan with technology, while Pakistan assisted the Chinese air force in expanding its operational experience by way of bilateral joint exercises like Shaheen.” He added that there were limits to the extent of China’s assistance, prompting Pakistan to move towards self-reliance.
Beyond reducing dependence on foreign suppliers, greater domestic production could also allow Pakistan to export its weapons systems. Fa’az could complement the JF-17 Thunder, which Pakistan is already exporting, giving prospective buyers the option of acquiring both the fighter aircraft and its accompanying air-to-air missile.
However, Air Marshal AK Bharti, Director General of Air Operations during Operation Sindoor, questioned Pakistan’s claim that the missile was indigenous. “The indigenous component of Fa’az should be taken with a pinch of salt, as they could very well just be assembling foreign components,” he told ThePrint.
Foreign technological influences in Pakistan’s indigenous missile inventory cannot be ruled out, given Islamabad’s longstanding defence ties with China. GIDS is also developing a longer-range missile, called Fa’az-2, in technological cooperation with Turkey’s TÜBİTAK SAGE, which is developing the country’s own air-to-air missile, GÖKDOĞAN.
Air Marshal Bharti said India should take note of the development regardless of how much of the missile is indigenous. “It is a capability with the adversary, however small it may be,” he said.
Recent clashes between India and Pakistan have predominantly involved beyond-visual-range (BVR) engagements. A defining feature of Operation Sindoor was that aircraft from neither India nor Pakistan crossed into each other’s airspace and the fighting occurred through long-range and BVR platforms.
“The next India-Pakistan standoff, as indeed an aerial battle anywhere in the world, would predominantly be a BVR combat, but you cannot do away with within-visual-range AAMs (WVRAAMs) completely,” Air Marshal Bharti told ThePrint.
Against this backdrop, it is important to take stock of the PAF’s existing BVRAAM inventory.
PL-12/SD-10A
Among the longer-range missiles in Pakistan’s inventory is the Chinese SD-10A BVRAAM, an export variant of the PL-12 missile. It is produced under licence by the Pakistan Aeronautical Complex and appears to have partly influenced Fa’az’s design.
A report by the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) said the PL-12 was China’s first indigenous active radar-guided air-to-air missile. It entered service with the Chinese Air Force and Navy in 2005.
The SD-10A is an active radar-guided BVRAAM fitted on Chinese combat aircraft, including the JF-17 Thunder. Its range is slightly lower than that of the PL-12 which, according to many estimates, has a maximum range of 100 km, with the export version having a maximum range of roughly 70 km.
PL-15E and Operation Sindoor
Another long-range missile in Pakistan’s inventory is the Chinese PL-15E, the export variant of the PL-15. It is integrated into the armament of the J-10C and JF-17 Block III fighters.
Designed as an advanced successor to the PL-12, the PL-15 is equipped with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar seeker. It is powered by a dual-pulse solid rocket motor and has a maximum speed of Mach 4–5 (supersonic).
The RUSI report notes that the PL-15 has a profile visually similar to the US-made AIM-120 C/D Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile (AMRAAM), but “outranges the latest AIM-120D model and has a comparable maximum range to the Meteor [French-made missile]”.
Pakistan was the first export customer for the PL-15E. Its first deployment came during the May 2025 confrontation with India, following the Pahalgam attack. Missile debris reportedly fell inside Indian territory in Hoshiarpur, Punjab. Air Marshal AK Bharti subsequently confirmed at a press briefing following Operation Sindoor that Pakistan had used the missile, pointing to its debris.
The PL-15E’s operational range caught the Indian Air Force (IAF) off guard, according to a Reuters report. Indian officials had estimated its range at approximately 150 km. The missile, however, struck an Indian aircraft from a distance of nearly 200 km during combat, Reuters reported.
American AAMs
For its fleet of American F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft, Pakistan relies on US-made AAMs, particularly the AIM-120C-5 AMRAAM. According to data from one of its operators, the AIM-120C-5 has a maximum range of around 74 km.
During the 2019 India-Pakistan confrontation following the Pulwama attack, India publicly displayed debris from an AIM-120C-5 as evidence that Pakistan had deployed its American-made F-16s against India.
“Pakistan claimed they did not use F-16. There is enough evidence to show that F-16s were used in this mission through their electronic signatures. Parts of AMRAAM air-to-air missile, which is carried only on the F-16s, was recovered east of Rajouri within Indian territory,” Air Vice Marshal R.G.K. Kapoor had said after the 2019 confrontation.
Air Marshal Diptendu Choudhury said the US had refused to acknowledge that Pakistan used F-16s against India, given Islamabad’s assurances that the aircraft would be used for counter-terrorism operations rather than against India.
Months after Operation Sindoor, the US confirmed the sale of AMRAAMs to Pakistan through defence manufacturer Raytheon. On 30 September 2025, the US Department of War issued a press release announcing contracts awarded to several American defence firms. The US Embassy in India subsequently confirmed the sale, but described it not as a new agreement to upgrade Pakistan’s existing capabilities, but as “an existing Foreign Military Sales contract for sustainment and spares for several countries, including Pakistan”.
Pakistan had earlier purchased 700 AAMs from US-based Raytheon in 2007. The order included 500 AMRAAMs, making it the largest international order for the weapon at the time, and 200 short-range AIM-9M Sidewinder missiles.
The bigger question here is whether Pakistan would deploy its American AMRAAM (and its F-16 fleet at large) against India again, even though the PAF’s large inventory of Chinese-AAMs provides enough alternatives to bypass American systems against India.
French and American short-range AAMs
The infrared-guided Sidewinder remains a short-range weapon of choice for Pakistan’s F-16 fleet. The PAF continues to operate the all-aspect AIM-9L and the older AIM-9P variants.
It also operates the French-made, infrared-guided Matra Magic 2 AAM, which is comparable to the AIM-9L and offers an alternative to the US-made weapon.
These short-range AAMs (SRAAMs) are primarily intended for within-visual-range (WVR) dogfights. Given the changing nature of aerial combat and the growing importance of BVRAAMs, their role in a future India-Pakistan confrontation may be more limited.
Implications for India
Air Marshal AK Bharti told ThePrint that India should take note of the development without being unduly alarmed. “Any new weapon the adversary gets will naturally be a cause of concern, but India need not be unduly alarmed by this development. Of course, India must continue to keep its eyes open and factor in each and every development across the border, in its larger scheme of things,” he said.
Given Pakistan’s asymmetry with India and its continued reliance on foreign suppliers, maintaining a substantial stockpile of AAMs remains critical for Islamabad. However, dependence on other countries poses both financial and geopolitical constraints and indigenous production could reduce the risk of the PAF depleting its BVRAAM supplies in the case of a prolonged conflict with India.
Air Marshal Choudhury said that, over and above the radar range, the missile’s range should be greater than the adversary’s. “India for the longest time, up until the Kargil war, had a BVR missile advantage over Pakistan. This advantage lay in the Indian Air Force’s AAM ability to outstick PAF’s.”
Put simply, the IAF’s missiles had a greater range than Pakistan’s weapons. By the 2019 Balakot strikes, however, Pakistan possessed more sophisticated AMRAAMs than India’s, the Air Marshal said.
India has its own indigenous BVRAAM family, Astra, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). The Astra Mk-1, with a range exceeding 100 kilometres, has already been inducted into the IAF. Its range is being extended, while the Astra Mk-2 is undergoing testing. Plans are also underway for the Astra Mk-3.
So, while Fa’az expanded the weapons options available to its Air Force, what will ultimately matter is whether Pakistan can match or exceed Indian missile ranges and how quickly it can produce and induct the missile into operational service.
India remains ahead of Pakistan in indigenous AAM development and has demonstrated this through its Astra programme.
Air Marshal Choudhury said, “There is a long way till Pakistan inducts Fa’az into its service. Nevertheless, India should keep up the pace and accelerate its own missile technology. It’s a cat-and-mouse game in which India should remain ahead of Pakistan both in terms of weapons capability and scalability. India should also widen its choices on the AAMs menu and should continue upgrading its missiles by increasing their ranges, and making them lighter and smarter.”
(Edited by Chingkheinganbi Mayengbam)
